strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed appearance addresses a limitation of single-modality retrieval. ITCPR provides a useful starting benchmark with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets.

Word4Per is a coherent, relatively lightweight approach. Domain adaptation followed by a frozen-encoder textual inversion stage enables composition without annotated CPR training triplets. The manuscript appropriately defines zero-shot relative to triplet supervision, while using existing identity-labeled image–text data.

The gains over simple fusion are substantial on the proposed benchmark. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.549% Rank-1 and 55.260% mAP, compared with 32.016% and 41.831% for fine-tuned image–text averaging. Improvements also hold with ViT-B/16.

The experiments cover supervision choices, training-data quantities and sources, network architectures, and fusion strategies. The supplementary material adds useful runtime measurements and qualitative examples. The pipeline is understandable, and the reported training settings support partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The principal comparison with Pic2Word is not adequately controlled. Table 1 explicitly states that its mapper was trained with original CLIP parameters, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This introduces an encoder–mapper mismatch and confounds domain adaptation with the proposed methodological improvement. Table 2 partially addresses this through an ITC ablation, but a clearly specified Pic2Word baseline retrained with the same encoders, data, and budget is needed to establish the claimed advance.

Methodological originality is limited. Mapping images into pseudo-word tokens for composed retrieval already appears in Pic2Word and the cited textual-inversion literature; the remaining components largely combine established person-retrieval training and matching losses. The identity-aware and text-supervised adaptation is useful, but the paper needs a sharper account of its distinct contribution and stronger comparisons with the closest approaches.

The evaluation does not establish independent model selection. Section 4.1 designates ITCPR exclusively for testing, yet Appendix C.3 selects optimal architectures from its results and subsequent experiments optimize data and fusion configurations on the same benchmark. No separate development protocol is described. This particularly weakens the optimized supplementary results. Repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are also absent, making smaller ablation and ensemble gains difficult to assess.

Benchmark validation and reproducibility need more detail. Appendix B.1 uses a visual encoder to retrieve annotation candidates, but does not specify the encoder, retrieval depth, annotator agreement, or an audit of remaining false negatives. The paper also lacks results separated by source dataset or degree of clothing change. Because construction deliberately retains some clothing cues, controlled examples involving similarly dressed different identities would help establish the identity-specific capability motivating CPR.

Some explanatory conclusions exceed the evidence. In Table 4, changing datasets and filtering by resolution changes sample count and data distribution alongside quality; matched-size random subsets are needed to isolate the claim that quality dominates quantity. The pseudo-word visualizations are informative illustrations, but provide limited evidence about which attributes survive composition or how conflicting clothing information is resolved.

Research ethics and dataset governance are underdocumented for a contribution explicitly motivated by surveillance and public security. The manuscript should explain permitted reuse and redistribution of the source data and discuss privacy, misuse, and false-identification harms. These omissions require attention, although the primary reasons for rejection are the comparison and evaluation weaknesses.
